title: What are JPA projections and their three forms (interface-based, class-based/DTO with constructor expression, dynamic), and why do they beat loading the full entity?
shortTitle: JPA projections three forms — interface, DTO constructor, dynamic — why they beat full entity

s1_definition.profdef: JPA projections select ONLY the columns your API response needs instead of loading every column of the entity. Three forms: (1) INTERFACE-BASED — declare a Java interface with getters for wanted fields; Spring maps only those columns via a runtime proxy. Supports SpEL `@Value` for computed values. (2) CLASS/DTO — a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new Dto(e.field1, e.field2) FROM Entity e`, or a record/class with matching constructor. No proxy — direct instantiation. (3) DYNAMIC — `<T> List<T> findBy(String x, Class<T> type)` lets the CALLER choose the projection at runtime. Projections beat full entity because: fewer columns transferred over the network, no persistence-context management (no snapshot, no dirty checking), lighter serialized JSON response, and reduced memory footprint. For a 20-column entity where the API needs 3 columns, projection reduces data transfer by 85%.
s1_definition.analogy: Full entity: the bank clerk photocopies Rajesh's ENTIRE 20-page customer file every time. Projection: the clerk writes ONLY name, account number, and balance on a slip — 3 fields instead of 20. Interface projection: the slip format is pre-printed (interface). DTO projection: the clerk fills a specific receipt form (record). Dynamic: Rajesh chooses which form he wants at the counter.
s1_definition.oneliner: Interface = proxy with getters + optional SpEL. DTO = constructor expression or record (fastest). Dynamic = Class<T> caller chooses. All beat full entity: fewer columns, no persistence context, lighter response.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JPA projections select ONLY the columns your API response needs instead of loading every column of the entity. Three forms: (1) INTERFACE-BASED — declare a Java interface with getters for wanted fields; Spring maps only those columns via a runtime proxy. Supports SpEL `@Value` for computed values. (2) CLASS/DTO — a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new Dto(e.field1, e.field2) FROM Entity e`, or a record/class with matching constructor. No proxy — direct instantiation. (3) DYNAMIC — `<T> List<T> findBy(String x, Class<T> type)` lets the CALLER choose the projection at runtime. Projections beat full entity because: fewer columns transferred over the network, no persistence-context management (no snapshot, no dirty checking), lighter serialized JSON response, and reduced memory footprint. For a 20-column entity where the API needs 3 columns, projection reduces data transfer by 85%.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Full entity: the bank clerk photocopies Rajesh's ENTIRE 20-page customer file every time. Projection: the clerk writes ONLY name, account number, and balance on a slip — 3 fields instead of 20. Interface projection: the slip format is pre-printed (interface). DTO projection: the clerk fills a specific receipt form (record). Dynamic: Rajesh chooses which form he wants at the counter.

**One line to remember:** Interface = proxy with getters + optional SpEL. DTO = constructor expression or record (fastest). Dynamic = Class<T> caller chooses. All beat full entity: fewer columns, no persistence context, lighter response.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's customer search API returns account data for the mobile app.** The Account entity has 20 columns including large BLOB (signature image) and TEXT (audit history) fields. The mobile app only shows: account ID, holder name, and balance. Loading full entities transfers signature images and audit history — 50x more data than needed. The API response is 5MB instead of 100KB. The team creates three projection options: interface with SpEL computed displayName for the search dropdown, DTO record for the account list (fastest), and dynamic projection for the admin panel where the operator chooses detail level (summary vs full).

**What the project will show:** Interface projection with SpEL @Value, DTO record projection (fastest), dynamic Class<T> projection, nested interface projection for account+trades, full entity comparison showing memory/network waste, and the 85% data transfer reduction.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Mobile app search: user types "Kumar". Controller calls `service.searchWithDto("Kumar")`.

**Step 2.** Repository `searchByName` has JPQL constructor: `SELECT new AccountOverview(a.accountId, a.holderName, a.balance) FROM Account a WHERE a.holderName LIKE '%Kumar%'`.

**Step 3.** Hibernate generates SQL: `SELECT account_id, holder_name, balance FROM accounts WHERE holder_name LIKE '%Kumar%'`. Only 3 columns — NOT phone, email, pan, aadhaar, address, audit_history, etc.

**Step 4.** ResultSet: 1 row. Hibernate calls `new AccountOverview("SAV2001", "Rajesh Kumar", 125000.50)`. Plain record — no proxy, no persistence context. Zero snapshot.

**Step 5.** Response JSON: `{"accountId":"SAV2001","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":125000.50}`. Size: ~80 bytes. Full entity response would include 15 fields + large TEXT fields = ~5KB per record. For 1000 search results: 80KB vs 5MB = 98% smaller response.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ FULL ENTITY vs PROJECTION ═══

  Full entity (15 columns):
    SELECT * FROM accounts → accountId, holderName, balance, phone, email,
                              pan, aadhaar, address, nominee, auditHistory, ...
    → 500 bytes per row + persistence context (snapshot + dirty checking)
    → 5MB for 10K rows + 5MB snapshots = 10MB total

  DTO projection (3 columns):
    SELECT account_id, holder_name, balance FROM accounts
    → 75 bytes per row + NO persistence context
    → 750KB for 10K rows + 0 snapshots = 750KB total
    → 93% less memory!

  ═══ INTERFACE vs DTO vs DYNAMIC ═══

  INTERFACE:
    + SpEL @Value for computed fields (displayName)
    + Nested projections (account → trades)
    - Proxy overhead (Spring generates proxy at runtime)

  DTO/RECORD:
    + Fastest (no proxy, direct constructor call)
    + Immutable (record)
    - No SpEL, no nested collection projections
    - Requires JPQL constructor expression for custom queries

  DYNAMIC:
    + Caller chooses projection at runtime
    + One repository method, many projections
    - Method signature less clear (Class<T> parameter)
```

```
  Projections fetch only required columns — less I/O, no managed-entity overhead.
  Interface (proxy), DTO constructor (JPQL new), dynamic (Class<T> param).
  Observability: bytes-scanned per query, projection vs full-entity latency.
  Security: projections expose a minimal field set — natural PII minimization.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Three Projection Forms (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DTO Pattern: thin read model decoupled from entity               │
  │  Strategy: interface vs class vs dynamic projection selection     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  I: clients depend only on the fields the projection exposes      │
  │  S: projection carries read shape; entity carries full state      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> AccountView  (interface proj.)    │
  │  getId():Long  getBalance():BigDecimal          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ record AccountDto(Long id,BigDecimal balance)   │ (DTO constructor)
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> AccountRepository                 │
  │  List<AccountView> findByBranch(String b);      │
  │  @Query("select new ...AccountDto(a.id,         │
  │     a.balance) from Account a")                 │
  │  List<AccountDto> findDtoByBranch(String b);    │
  │  <T> List<T> findByType(String t, Class<T> c);  │ ← dynamic
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠ Nested interface projections can re-trigger extra queries (N+1-like).
  Rule: flat read API → interface; explicit shape/mapping → DTO constructor.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
JPA projections fetch only the columns your API needs, dramatically reducing data transfer, memory, and CPU. Interface projections declare getter methods in an interface — Spring generates a proxy that maps only those columns. They uniquely support SpEL `@Value` for computed fields like `getDisplayName()`. DTO/record projections use a JPQL constructor expression — no proxy, direct object creation, fastest approach. Dynamic projections accept `Class<T>` as a parameter, letting the caller choose the shape at runtime.

In my customer search service, the Account entity has 15 columns including large TEXT fields (address, audit history). The mobile search API needs only 3 fields. DTO projection reduces data transfer by 85% — 75 bytes per row instead of 500. For 10,000 search results: 750KB instead of 5MB response. Plus zero persistence context overhead — no snapshots, no dirty checking. Interface projection adds SpEL for the search dropdown: `"Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001)"` computed at runtime without an extra DB column.

Projections beat full entities in three ways: network (fewer columns = less data transferred from DB to app), memory (no persistence context management = no snapshots, no dirty checking), and serialization (smaller JSON = faster API response). Always use projections for read-only API endpoints. Use full entities only when you need to UPDATE the data (dirty checking requires the full entity in the persistence context).
